item.title: Anthropic's IPO attracts $120 billion in retail demand, surpassing SpaceX
item.description: The AI firm's share sale attracted $115-120 billion in retail demand and more than $500 billion from institutional investors, even as its stock fell nearly 15 per cent on Friday ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Anthony Hughes Anthropic PBC’s initial public offering drew roughly between $115 billion and $120 billion of demand for shares from retail investors, according to a person familiar with the matter, more than the amount sought by them in SpaceX’s debut.  The frontier AI lab’s first-time share sale had well over $500 billion of demand from institutional investors, more than double the orders for shares in SpaceX, the person said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public. Anthropic’s IPO is the biggest of all time, with the $93.5 billion raised by the company and its seven co-founders, including the over-allotment, comfortably topping SpaceX’s $86.2 billion offering. Anthropic also raised $26 billion in a private placement, for a total haul of $119.5 billion. Even as the IPO delivered a record amount to the company, adding to the nearly $132 billion of cash and equivalents it had as of Sept. 30, Anthropic’s shares erased much of their first-day jump on Friday, testing investors’ faith after the AI lab delivered the biggest initial public offering in history. Shares of Anthropic fell as much as nearly 15 per cent on Friday, after the stock gained 17 per cent in its first trading day as a public company. The trading gives Anthropic a market value of about $1.5 trillion, ranking it among the 15 biggest publicly traded companies in the world. Most of the stock in Anthropic’s IPO went to long-only investors and sovereign wealth funds, with venture capital investors receiving a low-to-mid single digit percentage point share in aggregate, the person said. Banks working on the first-time share sale, led by Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Morgan Stanley, allocated fewer shares to investors relative to the size of the offering than those who placed orders for SpaceX’s IPO, they said. Retail investors in Anthropic’s IPO received about 15 per cent of the shares available, Bloomberg News reported.  Some of the details of the demand were previously reported by the International Financial Review and the Financial Times. Representatives for Anthropic, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley declined to comment. SpaceX’s IPO maintained its dominance in some corners of the retail universe. Demand for Anthropic’s IPO was second to SpaceX’s first-time share sale, still the record-holder on both Robinhood Markets Inc. and Charles Schwab Corp.’s platforms.  More than 360,000 people requested shares in the Anthropic IPO through Robinhood Financial and Trade PMR, and everyone who requested a share received at least one, if not more, a Robinhood spokesperson said. AI-related shares led activity on Schwab’s platform on Friday, with Anthropic among the top five names, according to a Schwab spokesperson. Anthropic’s IPO left more than half of the institutional investors bidding for stock without any shares, with allocations heavily skewed toward US-based investors, Bloomberg News reported. About 1,200 institutional investors placed orders, people familiar with the matter have said. The company sold $1.1 billion worth of stock to retail investors in the UK and continental Europe, and raised about $3 billion in Japan and around $110 million in Australia, Bloomberg News has reported. The 22 banks on Anthropic’s IPO earned a record $550 million in fees for their work, more than on SpaceX’s IPO. They didn’t receive fees for the so-called over-allotment shares, or for the private placement shares, according to its filings. Demand for SpaceX shares ran to more than $350 billion, with over $100 billion coming from retail, people familiar with the matter said at the time. Anthropic’s listing joins companies linked to AI that have lifted US IPO volume to an all-time high. First time stock sales raised $258 billion this year, beating 2021’s $195 billion haul, excluding financial vehicles such as blank-check firms, data compiled by Bloomberg show.  Anthropic won over investors with a focus on enterprise customers, propelling its run-rate revenue — a measure annualized from a shorter period — to $81 billion as of Oct. 31, up $10 billion from the end of September, its regulatory filings show. Claude Code, the company’s coding agent for software developers, is widely adopted in the industry and has even been used by NASA engineers, the filing shows. Anthropic has more than 11,900 customers delivering $100,000 of revenue each on a trailing 12-month basis as of the end of September, up from about 1,500 in 2025. Anthropic and its rival OpenAI face mounting public scrutiny over AI safety after a string of high-profile hacking incidents by rogue agents, and as the debate rages over whether the technology poses what Anthropic called “existential risks to humanity” in its IPO filing. OpenAI has filed confidentially for a listing but isn’t planning to go public before 2027.

item.title: Jensen Huang should return as Nvidia CEO after 'big apology', says Trump
item.description: Trump said Huang deserved a second chance, despite Nvidia's board indicating it had no plans to reinstate the former chief executive, with interim CEO Colette Kress seeking to reassure employees ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Josh Wingrove and Courtney Subramanian President Donald Trump called for Jensen Huang to make a big apology and return as chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., even as the prospect remains highly unlikely. The Nvidia board has indicated they don’t intend to bring back the embattled former CEO, but Trump on Friday continued to insist that the return would be a good idea because he is “one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world.” He reiterated at a White House press conference that his own pick to replace Huang is Apple Inc.’s Tim Cook but added that he “would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know we’re a country of second chances.” “I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back,” Trump said. “He put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies.”  While Trump joins Silicon Valley figures close to Huang, including billionaire Elon Musk, in calling for the former CEO’s return, the board has dismissed the idea and interim CEO Colette Kress looked to reassure staff at a town hall about the company’s future after the ouster.  Allegations in a California lawsuit filed in 2007 show that Nvidia employees’ complaints about how Huang treated his staff — including allegations that he threatened them and made sexually explicit remarks — date back decades. Trump said he discussed the Nvidia matter with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a meeting in Shenzhen earlier this week, saying his counterpart also called Huang “brilliant.” The US president also compared Huang to Musk, saying he was “very proud of protecting Elon in my first term” and that he continues to do “pretty amazing” things.  The revelations that Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who worked at a Singapore-based firm that obtained advanced chips from his company loomed over the leaders’ sitdowns.  That tumult allowed infighting among US administration officials over China policy and the enforcement of curbs on semiconductor exports to spill into the open, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent openly blaming the Commerce Department, led by Secretary Howard Lutnick, for not acting to prevent China from obtaining the advanced technology.   Bessent cited Commerce’s failure to add the Singapore-based firm, Megaspeed International, to the entity list that would have cut it off from sensitive US technology. Lutnick also has been called to testify before Congress about his relationship with Nvidia. Trump has continued to back Lutnick despite the criticism, asserting Friday in response to a question that he had not lost confidence in his Commerce secretary. He told reporters on Monday before leaving for his four-day trip to the Philippines and China that Lutnick had “done a very good job” and may have stalled restrictions to avoid further conflict with Beijing. Amid the scrutiny, the Commerce Department on Monday sought to limit several countries from providing Chinese companies remote access to advance AI chip and servers, a move likely to anger Beijing and regional partners. China has warned the US over those restrictions, and Beijing is seen to be already mulling some retaliation. The US president has repeatedly dismissed concerns that the fallout from the Nvidia scandal compromised US national security, telling reporters before his trip, “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”

item.title: No further curbs needed on Nvidia chip sales to China: US Treasury secy
item.description: Bessent said existing restrictions and curbs on remote access to advanced semiconductors were sufficient, a day after lawmakers flagged approvals for over 850,000 Nvidia and AMD chips to Chinese firms ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / No further curbs needed on Nvidia chip sales to China: US Treasury secy

No further curbs needed on Nvidia chip sales to China: US Treasury secy Bessent said existing restrictions and curbs on remote access to advanced semiconductors were sufficient, a day after lawmakers flagged approvals for over 850,000 Nvidia and AMD chips to Chinese firms

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent | Image: Bloomberg

AP Washington 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 21 2026 | 8:00 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said no further restrictions on the sale of older Nvidia chips to China are needed following the Trump administration's move earlier this week to block China's remote access to the latest semiconductors. The ability of Chinese tech firms to access Nvidia's technology came under scrutiny after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down amid allegations of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that uses advanced chips to generate computing power that Chinese firms access remotely. "The proper chip restrictions are in place," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC on Friday after returning from a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump. "And the remote access has been curtailed."   Bessent's comments came a day after the House Foreign Affairs Committee released details of the Commerce Department's approval of the sales of more than 850,000 chips from Nvidia and its competitor AMD to Chinese companies. The Pentagon has identified some of those companies as having ties to the Chinese military.

The report tracked applications from Nvidia to sell its H200 chips -- one of its more powerful products, though not the most advanced -- and AMD's applications to sell its roughly comparable MI325X chip to companies that are either located or headquartered in China, or entities with parent companies based in China. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security approved the export, re-export, or transfer of 879,868 of these chips to companies with Chinese ties across 21 license applications as of May 11, 2026, the report said. Nvidia and AMD had requested to sell a cumulative total of more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese-tied companies across those applications, per the report.

Also Read

The approvals, which don't necessarily indicate completed sales, included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent and its subsidiaries, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, according to the report. Each of those companies has been identified by the Defense Department as having ties to the Chinese military. The report shows the Commerce Department has a "long track record of transparency with Congress about licensing activity for the H200 and equivalent chips, including both approvals and rejections", a spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security said in a statement Friday. The spokesperson said the Commerce Department's approach to H200 licensing is based on a rule in the Federal Register that was published in January. The rule imposes "significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial," the spokesperson said.

An Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement on Friday that the "limited shipments we made under the H200 programme were legal and authorised" by the BIS. "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes," the company spokesperson said. Earlier this week, Nvidia said it was no longer shipping H200 chips to China. The spokesperson said on Friday that shipments had stopped despite prior approvals. AMD said it complies with US export control laws and regulations and maintains "rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations" in a statement from a spokesperson Friday. "We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity," the spokesperson said.

Chinese technology firms have been bracing for impacts on their ambitious AI development plans as scrutiny mounts on export controls in the US. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under intense scrutiny himself in the wake of the turmoil following the Huang affair. Last week, Bessent said he was frustrated with the Commerce Department's delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the US for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. A former executive at the company who allegedly had an affair with Huang was reportedly suspected by US intelligence agencies of being a spy for China.

In an unusually public rebuke of a fellow Cabinet member, Bessent said his department wanted to place export controls on Megaspeed, but Commerce was in charge of the matter. Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump said he has "not lost confidence" in Lutnick. Calling him a "different kind of guy," Trump said he "has a natural business instinct" and has "done a very good job".

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.description: A New York federal judge said the plaintiffs failed to show that taxpayer-funded advertisements were still causing imminent and irreparable harm after the November 3 midterm elections ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US judge declines long-term ban on Trump admin's taxpayer-funded ads

US judge declines long-term ban on Trump admin's taxpayer-funded ads A New York federal judge said the plaintiffs failed to show that taxpayer-funded advertisements were still causing imminent and irreparable harm after the November 3 midterm elections

The incremental victory for the Trump administration comes as a parallel case unfolds in Washington, DC | Image Credit: Bloomberg

AP New York 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 21 2026 | 7:52 AM IST

Listen to This Article

A federal judge has declined to issue a long-term ban on the Trump administration's controversial taxpayer-funded political advertisements, leaving their future in the hands of a different judge who is overseeing a similar case. US District Judge Jennifer L Rochon in New York argued on Friday that the suing coalition, which includes the government watchdog group Common Cause, didn't convincingly prove the ads were still causing them "imminent and irreparable harm" now that November's midterm elections are over. "The urgency of the earlier requests for temporary injunctive relief in this case centered around the November 3, 2026, midterm and state elections," Rochon wrote in a court filing. "Those elections have now passed."   The incremental victory for the Trump administration comes as a parallel case unfolds in Washington, DC.

In that case, the Democratic National Committee has asked the court for a preliminary injunction to stop the Trump administration from developing, distributing or airing the ads. The judge hasn't yet ruled on that matter after a hearing earlier this week. At issue in Friday's ruling were TV spots the Trump administration started airing in September that were paid for at least in part by a USD 20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. Also Read

Some of the ads glorified the president with highlight reels of scenic speeches and callouts about tax cuts and support for law enforcement. One of them repurposed a clip that had been used by Trump's 2024 presidential campaign, showing him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a "final battle" against "globalists" and "warmongers."   Some of the ads also appeared on Trump administration social media channels and the White House website.

The plaintiffs had argued the ads were illegal government-sponsored propaganda intended to promote the president's campaign message just weeks before Election Day. The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements. The judges in both cases issued temporary restraining orders blocking some of the ads in the lead-up to the election. A temporary restraining order in the Democrats' case expires next week. Bradley Girard, senior counsel at Democracy Forward, which represented the plaintiffs in the New York case, said while the team is disappointed, "we will continue to pursue this case on the merits to prevent this from happening in the future."   The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
